newsitem.title: POLAND: ZLOTY FATE HINGES ON FLOOD SPENDING IMPACT.
newsitem.headline: ZLOTY FATE HINGES ON FLOOD SPENDING IMPACT.

text.p: The zloty's near-term fate hinges on the impact of government flood relief spending on Poland's current account and inflation, and until this is clear investors may stay bearish on the currency, analysts said.
On Tuesday the zloty plummeted five percent against the basket of currencies to 5.69 percent below the parity without any objections from the central bank.
It made a partial recovery on Wednesday thanks to a small central bank currency selling intervention to a fixing of 3.41 percent, but analysts said its problems were far from over.
"It's hard to see any light on the horizon for the zloty," said Robert Beange, economist at Lehman Brothers in London.

"The private sector will have to replace or repair a lot of the flood damage and this will put additional pressure on the balance of payments. Until the impact of the floods on the balance of payments is clear we are going to get very worried that it will grow beyond sustainable proportions," Beange said.
Poland's current account gap grew to $2.4 billion after the first five months of this year against $1.35 billion or one pecent of GDP in the whole of 1996.

The finance ministry estimates it will widen to 3-3.5 percent of GDP in 1997 on balooning domestic demand, which the central bank so far unsuccessfully tried to dampen by raising banks' mandatory reserves and through small market rate rises.
Some analysts said the bearish zloty mood was more a result of uncertainty over what effects the flood relief money would have on the economy, than concern over hard data.

"Every new piece of information which investors are able to use for their calculations is likely to reduce this uncertainty and help the zloty," said Piotr Las, analyst at Creditanstalt Securities in Warsaw.
A week of torrential rains caused floods in south-western Poland which put 4,000 sq km of Poland under water killing at least 39 and forcing tens of thousands out of their homes.

To deal with the aftermath of the disaster the government seeks a 2.5 billion zloty credit line from the central bank and $300 million World Bank loan after it had already squeezed 650 million zlotys from exisiting budget resources.

The government stresses that the 2.5 billion zlotys would stay within the limits of the planned spending in 1997, and that it wanted to borrow from the central bank, and not on the market, to maintain liqudity at a difficult time.

The National Bank of Poland so far said it was ready to support the government only with a one billion zloty loan at market rates and that it would collect deposits to offset the inflationary impulse such a credit would create.
"With the poor inflation figures yesterday, and the flood is going to make them worse, it's hard to see where good news is going to come from," Lehman's Beange said.
On Tuesday the Central Statistical Office said Poland's year-on-year inflation rose to 15.3 percent in June from 14.6 percent in May. The target for December is 13 percent.

Analysts said the central bank could kill two birds with one stone if it raised its nominal interest rates, because it would at the same time defend the zloty and cool domestic demand without attracting speculative foreign inflows.
"The reason for not raising rates in recent months has been the fear of speculative foreign inflows and that is hardly a problem now," said Andrew Kenningham, economist at Merrill Lynch in London.
"They may take the opportunity to raise rates, which would show support for the currency and help dampen domestic demand," Kenningham said. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
